result:
Neither, as things stand. The premise is the problem: more agents does not always give better results.

Think of a group project. Five people on a task that one person could finish means more meetings, more handoffs and more things lost in translation. Agents work the same way. Each one has its own context, so every handoff is a message that can drop detail. Each one also makes its own model calls, so cost goes up. Anthropic's write-up on their multi-agent research system says multi-agent setups use roughly 15× the tokens of a plain chat. Please check that figure at the source before you quote it at your review. Your sponsor's budget is small, so this matters.

Splitting pays off when the work is broad and can run in parallel, or when one agent's context would overflow. It does badly when steps depend on each other, which is how most of your assistant's work goes. Booking is a good example. It reads the calendar, picks a slot, then writes the booking. Each step needs the one before it.

For your three jobs, one agent with three well-described tools is the sensible default. Answering from manuals and checking the calendar are tool calls, not separate agents. The booking step may be better as a fixed workflow. You would split only if you could measure that a single agent fails, for example because its context fills up with long manuals.

So the question to bring to your team is "what specific problem would a second agent solve?" The numbers five and ten don't answer that.

Quick check: which of your three jobs could run at the same time without needing each other's results?

If you'd like, I can write a lesson on workflows versus agents and when multi-agent pays off.

Source: Anthropic, "How we built our multi-agent research system" and "Building effective agents."
